item.title: Comment on How should government disclosure be done? by Ricardo
item.description:
Reply to Transparent is good:

At least the Trump Administration is transparently ending DOJ weaponization. "The Justice Department on Monday told federal prosecutors in New York to drop corruption charges against Mayor Eric Adams, saying his trial could interfere with his reelection bid and ability to focus on fighting crime and illegal immigration.

The memo from acting deputy attorney general Emil Bove said the decision was not based on the evidence or theory of the case against Adams, who was indicted in September and accused of being under illegal foreign influence and accepting bribes through campaign donations and luxury travel perks.

Instead, Bove made the unusual argument that Adams — who has made a point of aligning himself with President Donald Trump in recent months — should be free “to devote full attention and resources” to addressing illegal immigration and violent crime in New York City."

Leading to disloyal leftist lawyers resigning from their DOJ job. Like Danielle Sassoon, a registered Republican; participant in the Federalist Society; former law clerk to two conservative luminaries — federal appeals court judge J. Harvie Wilkinson III and the late Supreme Court justice Antonin Scalia, appointed by Trump three weeks ago.

She had the absolute gall to write this about her disloyalty to her boss and the president. “Both men instilled in me a sense of duty to contribute to the public good and uphold the rule of law, and a commitment to reasoned and thorough analysis,” Sassoon wrote in the letter, referring to Wilkinson and Scalia. “I cannot fulfill my obligations, effectively lead my office in carrying out the Department’s priorities, or credibly represent the Government before the courts, if I seek to dismiss the Adams case on this record.”

Thankfully, the Trump official who made plain that prosecution of Adams was something that the Trump Administration did not want to happen, let her know how things are today in America. “You lost sight of the oath that you took when you started at the Department of Justice by suggesting that you retain discretion to interpret the Constitution in a manner inconsistent with the policies of a democratically elected President and a Senate-confirmed Attorney General,” he wrote, according to a copy of the letter obtained by The Washington Post."

Can you imagine that someone appointed by Trump would write such nonsense? "In her letter, Sassoon described a Jan. 31 meeting with Bove and Adams’s attorneys. She said the mayor’s lawyers “repeatedly urged what amounted to a quid pro quo,” saying Adams could help with the Justice Department’s immigration priorities only if the indictment were dismissed.

“Rather than be rewarded, Adams’s advocacy should be called out for what it is: an improper offer of immigration enforcement assistance in exchange for a dismissal of his case,” Sassoon wrote. “Although Mr. Bove disclaimed any intention to exchange leniency in this case for Adams’s assistance in enforcing federal law, that is the nature of the bargain laid bare in Mr. Bove’s memo."

Worse, this guy, a decorated Iraq War veteran and Harvard Law School graduate who clerked for Chief Justice John G. Roberts Jr. and for Supreme Court Justice Brett M. Kavanaugh, was nothing but contemptuous of the Trump Administration. "“Any assistant U.S. attorney would know that our laws and traditions do not allow using the prosecutorial power to influence other citizens, much less elected officials, in this way,” he wrote.

“If no lawyer within earshot of the President is willing to give him that advice, then I expect you will eventually find someone who is enough of a fool, or enough of a coward, to file your motion,” Scotten’s letter said. “But it was never going to be me.”

We are lucky to get rid of such people, because a new dawn is arising in America, where the guiding principle of freedom is doing what the president orders.

In other words, crime is now legal as long as you are an elected official who falls in line with the President's policy agenda. I was half expecting Trump to pardon Eric Adams eventually because of all of the right-wing rhetoric about him supposedly being a victim of selective prosecution. But directly interfering in the prosecution in exchange for political favors and policy concessions is a new low. With a pardon, the President at least takes personal accountability for the fact that he is overturning the results of due process.

item.title: Comment on AI Personality Extraction from Faces: Labor Market Implications by Marie
item.description:
This is the kind of "AI application" that is really dangerous...

The danger comes from the fact that 1) there's no connection between the AI's "judgements" and reality -- "I can't tell you what the five traits are". That means there's nothing to "reality check". And human judgement is built on thousands of years "reality check" at a social evolution level, plus years of "reality check" on a personal level. Moreover, human judgement is resilient to error because there's tons of diversity -- everyone's judgements are (occasionally a lot) different...

I prefer a society where you sometimes lose because "someone doesn't like your face" (and sometimes succeed when someone does) to one where success is determined by an *inherently* incomprehensible standard for what is a "good" face.

2) When used this way, the AI creates its own reality and people necessarily *train themselves *to it. When we use AI to influence our judgements, a "good" essay or a "good face" or a "good" job interview or "valid" application for benefits is whatever the AI says it is. And people who succeed best will have effectively *trained themselves* to the AI. Making the AI even more apparently correct...

This is where you get the situation where the Swedish government "uses AI" to detect benefit fraud: There's no sensible way to appeal a decision, because there's no specific evidence or reason that can be investigated or disputed. There's just "something" in the huge mass of data -- and we convince ourselves that because it comes from a computer that it must be right (or at least must be obeyed by workers).

In the worst cast, this is how we end up with people in nightmare scenarios where they lose benefits, or get falsely arrested on some unlucky match in a database. Even in the best case, we end up with a mishmash of random speculation about what "gets past the AI"... from "the lipstick shade you should NEVER wear in job interview video" to €2000 AI-friendly facial contouring...
